Plitt & Giocomo (2021) on dandiset 000054, part 2: population codes and inference¶

Paper. Plitt MH, Giocomo LM (2021). Experience-dependent contextual codes in the hippocampus. Nature Neuroscience 24, 705-714. doi:10.1038/s41593-021-00816-6. The claims file was written from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC8893323) with its Methods, legends and supplementary information.

Dandiset. DANDI:000054, version 0.260415.1712, the most recent published version; the paper cites only the draft, and the 2021 versions hold 10 of the 16 mice (see part 1, 01_sessions_place_cells.ipynb, for the choice and the data check of every file).

This notebook tests the population similarity, SF, Q estimate and model claims. The priors (M7) need every trial a mouse ran before session 8; the dandiset holds only the imaged trials of the imaging sessions. Following the answer of 2026-10-22 (questions/plitt-2021.yaml), the priors are built from the authors' "Unprocessed VR data" on figshare (doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.31974756.v1), which holds every VR session, read by HTTP range requests into memory, file by file. Its mice are named by alias; the aliases of R1 to F6 are taken from the 2026 code (src/morph_analyses/mouse_metadata.py at commit 9230b0a of https://github.com/GiocomoLab/PlittGiocomo_2021). The link claim vr-deposit-link tests the match of its sessions to the dandiset's files, and training-intermediate-fraction uses the deposit alone (data: elsewhere). Claims whose posteriors or priors use it are data: with_inputs, and fig7-model-reproduces-remapping, which needs nothing else, is data: elsewhere. The earlier run's priors from the dandiset's imaged trials are shown as a variant, to show what the answer changed.

import time
import warnings
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

import morph as M

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
pd.set_option("display.width", 220)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 300)
started = time.time()

assets = M.asset_table()
print(f"dandiset {M.DANDISET_ID} version {M.DANDISET_VERSION}: {len(assets)} NWB files; paths the file-name pattern "
      f"does not read: {len(assets.attrs['unmatched'])}")
rf = assets.group != "decision"
pop = M.process_many([r for _, r in assets[rf & (assets.kind == "testing")].iterrows()], "population")
print(f"rare and frequent sessions 8 to N: {len(pop)} streamed in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
sfs = M.process_many([r for _, r in assets[(~rf) | (rf & (assets.kind == "training") & (assets.day == 3))].iterrows()], "sf")
print(f"decision mice (all sessions) and session 3 of rare and frequent mice: {len(sfs)}; {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
meta = M.process_many([r for _, r in assets[rf & (assets.kind == "training") & (assets.day != 3)].iterrows()], "meta", workers=8)
print(f"other training files, trials only: {len(meta)}; total {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
vr_ses, vr_trials = M.vr_deposit()
print(f"VR deposit {M.VR_DEPOSIT['doi']}: {len(vr_ses)} sessions of the 12 mice on {M.VR_TRACK}; total {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
RARE = ["R1", "R2", "R3", "R4", "R5", "R6"]
FREQ = ["F1", "F2", "F3", "F4", "F5", "F6"]
GROUP = {**{m: "rare" for m in RARE}, **{m: "frequent" for m in FREQ}}

                     "cells": s["n_cells"], "trials": len(s["trials"]), "frames": s["n_frames"],

vr-deposit-link¶

The sessions of the authors' VR deposit on figshare can be matched to the dandiset's imaging sessions of the rare and frequent morph mice, by mouse alias and trial sequence.

A link claim added by this attempt (protocol, Author 1.4): the priors of this notebook and training-intermediate-fraction take the deposit's sessions of each mouse before its session 8, so the deposit's mice and dates have to be those of the dandiset's files.

nwb_rf = [s for s in allsess if s["group"] != "decision"]
named = [s for s in allsess for a in M.ALIAS.values()
         if a in " ".join([str(s["subject"]), s["session_id"], str(s["json_mouse"]), s["description"]])]
print("NWB files whose subject, session id, annotation or description name a deposit alias:", len(named))
link = M.link_sessions(nwb_rf, vr_ses, vr_trials)
print("Deposit, the 12 mice on the task track: files", len(vr_ses), "; listed twice in the session database:",
      int((vr_ses.db_rows > 1).sum()), "; listed but missing from the zip:", int((~vr_ses.in_zip).sum()),
      "; trials without a morph value:", int(vr_ses.trials_no_morph.sum()))
print(vr_ses.groupby("mouse").agg(files=("member", "size"), trials=("trials", "sum"), first=("date", "min"),
                                  last=("date", "max"), imaging_flag=("Imaging", lambda x: int((x == 1).sum()))).to_string())
print("\nEach NWB file against every deposit file (S-tilde and the three jitters within 1e-4, as one contiguous run):")
print(link[["mouse", "kind", "day", "part", "nwb_trials", "matches", "other_mouse_matches", "member", "offset",
            "vr_trials", "max_diff"]].to_string(index=False))
one = (link.matches == 1) & (link.other_mouse_matches == 0)
print(f"\nNWB files of the 12 mice: {len(link)}; matching exactly one file of their own mouse and none of another: "
      f"{int(one.sum())} ({one.mean():.0%})")
print("Matched file holds exactly the NWB trials (offset 0, same count):",
      int(((link.offset == 0) & (link.vr_trials == link.nwb_trials)).sum()), "of", len(link),
      "; largest difference of S-tilde or jitter:", float(link.max_diff.max()))
print("Matched files carry the database's imaging flag:", int((link.imaging == 1).sum()), "of", len(link))
print("Matched files are distinct:", link.member.nunique() == len(link))
d8 = link[link.day == 8].set_index("mouse")[["date", "session_number", "member"]]
print("\nSession 8 of each mouse in the deposit (the NWB file of day 8):")
print(d8.to_string())
img = vr_ses[(vr_ses.Imaging == 1) & ~vr_ses.member.isin(link.member)]
print("\nDeposit files with the imaging flag that match no NWB file:", len(img))
print(img.groupby("mouse").agg(files=("member", "size"), trials=("trials", "sum"),
                               dates=("DateFolder", lambda d: " ".join(sorted(set(d))))).to_string())

# Session numbers (verifier's request for edf7): the file name's day against the ordinal of the matched
# deposit file's date among the mouse's dates on the task track in the deposit (one session a day).
dates = {m: sorted(vr_ses[vr_ses.mouse == m].date.unique()) for m in RARE + FREQ}
link["date_ordinal"] = [dates[r.mouse].index(r.date) + 1 for r in link.itertuples()]
link["sessions_that_date"] = [int(((vr_ses.mouse == r.mouse) & (vr_ses.date == r.date)).sum()) for r in link.itertuples()]
print("File day against the ordinal of its deposit date, per mouse (day:ordinal; * where they differ):")
for m, d in link.sort_values(["mouse", "day", "part"]).groupby("mouse"):
    print(f"  {m}:", " ".join(f"{dd}:{o}" + ("*" if dd != o else "") for dd, o in zip(d.day, d.date_ordinal)))
print("files whose day equals the date ordinal:", int((link.day == link.date_ordinal).sum()), "of", len(link),
      "; matched files on a date with more than one task-track file in the deposit:", int((link.sessions_that_date > 1).sum()))
print("task-track dates in the deposit before each mouse's first NWB file of day 8 that have no NWB file:",
      {m: int(sum(1 for dt in dates[m] if dt < link[(link.mouse == m) & (link.day == 8)].date.iloc[0]
                  and dt not in set(link[link.mouse == m].date))) for m in RARE + FREQ})
# The 2020 code's sessions 8 to N (SFReg: imaging sessions of the mouse, region CA1 or empty, from index first_sessions on,
# 5 5 5 3 5 2 for R1 to R6 and 4 for the frequent mice), found in the deposit's database and matched to the NWB files.
first_ind = dict(zip(RARE + FREQ, [5, 5, 5, 3, 5, 2] + [4] * 6))
code_rows = []
for m in RARE + FREQ:
    im = vr_ses[(vr_ses.mouse == m) & (vr_ses.Imaging == 1)]
    if "ImagingRegion" in im:
        im = im[im.ImagingRegion.fillna("").isin(["CA1", ""])]
    im = im.sort_values(["date", "SessionNumber"]).iloc[first_ind[m]:]
    for r in im.itertuples():
        hit = link[link.member == r.member]
        code_rows.append({"mouse": m, "member": r.member, "nwb_day": int(hit.day.iloc[0]) if len(hit) else None,
                          "nwb_trials": int(hit.nwb_trials.iloc[0]) if len(hit) else None})
code_s = pd.DataFrame(code_rows)
ours = link[link.kind == "testing"]
for g, mice in (("rare", RARE), ("frequent", FREQ)):
    cs = code_s[code_s.mouse.isin(mice)]
    print(f"{g}: the 2020 code's selection holds {len(cs)} sessions, {cs.nwb_day.notna().sum()} with an NWB file "
          f"({int(cs.nwb_trials.sum())} trials; the code printed 2540 rare and 1986 frequent); days of those with a file:",
          cs.dropna().groupby("mouse").nwb_day.apply(lambda d: [int(x) for x in d]).to_dict())
    o = ours[ours.mouse.isin(mice)]
    extra = o[~o.member.isin(cs.member)]
    print(f"   NWB sessions 8 to N not in the code's selection: {[(r.mouse, r.day) for r in extra.itertuples()]}")

Result: reproduced. All 89 NWB files of the 12 rare and frequent morph mice match exactly one deposit file of their own mouse, under the 2026 code's alias, and no file of another mouse; in every one the deposit file holds exactly the NWB trials (offset 0, same count), with S-tilde and the three jitters identical, and every matched file carries the database's imaging flag. So the deposit's aliases and dates are those of the dandiset's mice and sessions, and session 8 of each mouse has a date in the deposit. The deposit holds more than the dandiset: every session without imaging, R6's sessions before session 8, and further files with the imaging flag that match no NWB file (table above). No NWB file names a deposit alias, so the mapping of the aliases to the mice comes from the 2026 code alone; the trial sequences confirm it.

Session numbers (the cell after the result). The file name's day equals the ordinal of the matched file's date among the mouse's task-track dates in the deposit for 60 of the 89 files. For R1 to R4, R6 and F4 the imaging sessions 8 to N fall one date later (two for R6): the deposit holds eight task-track dates before session 8 for these mice (nine for R6), one more than sessions 1 to 7 (two more for R6). The paper's session numbers are read as the file days, which equal the annotation's day; the date ordinal is a second numbering, and the deposit does not say which the paper used. The 2020 code's selection of sessions 8 to N, rebuilt from the deposit's imaging flags, holds every NWB session 8 to N and more sessions with the flag (33 rare, 24 frequent), and its NWB trials (2,880 and 2,181) do not match the code's printed 2,540 and 1,986, so it does not identify the two extra rare sessions the dandiset holds against the paper's 24.

training-intermediate-fraction¶

Before session 8, rare morph mice had fewer than 4% of trials with intermediate morph values, while frequent morph mice had 60%.

Answer of 2026-10-22: the trials come from the figshare deposit (data: elsewhere), which holds every session. Trials before session 8 are those of every session on the task track on a date before the date of session 8 (vr-deposit-link), and of the earlier session numbers of that date. The variants do not decide: the 2026 code's two choices (sessions with more than 40 rewards; the sessions within 8 calendar days of the mouse's first), and the imaged trials the dandiset holds, which decided nothing in the earlier run either.

def before8(m):
    return M.sessions_before(vr_ses, m, d8.loc[m, "date"], d8.loc[m, "session_number"])


def first8(m):
    s = vr_ses[vr_ses.mouse == m]
    return s[(s.date - s.date.min()).dt.days < 8]


variants = {"every trial before session 8": before8,
            "code: more than 40 rewards": lambda m: before8(m)[before8(m).RewardCount > 40],
            "code 2026: within 8 days of the first": first8}
rows = []
for vname, f in variants.items():
    for m in RARE + FREQ:
        b = f(m)
        t = pd.concat([vr_trials[x] for x in b.member]).dropna(subset=["morph"])
        rows.append({"variant": vname, "group": "rare" if m in RARE else "frequent", "mouse": m, "sessions": len(b),
                     "days": b.date.nunique(), "trials": len(t), "intermediate": int(t.morph.isin([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]).sum())})
tf = pd.DataFrame(rows)
tf["fraction"] = (tf.intermediate / tf.trials).round(4)
early = tr[(tr.day < 8) & (tr.group != "decision")]
for m in RARE + FREQ:
    t = early[early.mouse == m]
    rows.append({"variant": "dandiset imaged trials", "group": "rare" if m in RARE else "frequent", "mouse": m,
                 "sessions": t.day.nunique(), "days": t.day.nunique(), "trials": len(t),
                 "intermediate": int(((t.morph > 0.01) & (t.morph < 0.99)).sum())})
tf = pd.DataFrame(rows)
tf["fraction"] = np.where(tf.trials > 0, tf.intermediate / tf.trials.clip(lower=1), np.nan).round(4)
print("Per mouse, sessions, days, trials and fraction with S-tilde 0.25, 0.5 or 0.75 before session 8:")
print(tf.pivot(index="mouse", columns="variant", values="fraction").loc[RARE + FREQ].to_string())
print(tf[tf.variant == "every trial before session 8"][["mouse", "sessions", "days", "trials", "intermediate"]].to_string(index=False))
print("\nS-tilde values in the deposit trials before session 8:",
      sorted(set(pd.concat([vr_trials[x] for m in RARE + FREQ for x in before8(m).member]).morph.dropna())))
res = []
for vname in tf.variant.unique():
    x = tf[tf.variant == vname]
    for g in ("rare", "frequent"):
        y = x[(x.group == g) & (x.trials > 0)]
        res.append({"variant": vname, "group": g, "a: pooled": round(y.intermediate.sum() / y.trials.sum(), 4),
                    "b: lowest mouse": y.fraction.min(), "b: highest mouse": y.fraction.max()})
res = pd.DataFrame(res)
print("\n" + res.to_string(index=False))
for vname in tf.variant.unique():
    r = res[res.variant == vname].set_index("group")
    ok_a = r.loc["rare", "a: pooled"] < 0.04 and abs(r.loc["frequent", "a: pooled"] - 0.6) <= 0.06
    ok_b = r.loc["rare", "b: highest mouse"] < 0.04 and abs(r.loc["frequent", "b: lowest mouse"] - 0.6) <= 0.06 \
        and abs(r.loc["frequent", "b: highest mouse"] - 0.6) <= 0.06
    print(f"{vname}: reading (a) holds {ok_a}; reading (b) holds {ok_b}")

Result: reproduced. From every trial the deposit holds before session 8, 3.49% of the rare morph mice's trials pooled (340 of 9,753) and 59.8% of the frequent morph mice's (5,700 of 9,527) are intermediate, so reading (a) holds: below 4%, and within 0.06 of 60%. Reading (b) does not, as R4 (4.1%) and R6 (5.7%) are above 4%; the frequent morph mice range from 59.2% to 60.6%. The 2026 code's variants give the same under reading (a) (3.41% and 3.19% rare, 59.8% and 59.8% frequent). The imaged trials the dandiset holds give 13.8% for the rare morph mice, as the earlier run found; the answer replaced them with the deposit.

Priors and posteriors (M7, M8)¶

Priors (M7): every trial each mouse ran before session 8, from the authors' VR deposit on figshare (answer of 2026-10-22). The deposit's sessions are matched to the dandiset's files as in vr-deposit-link above; session 8's date and session number in the deposit mark the end of the trials that enter the prior.

Every NWB file of the 12 mice matches one deposit file of its mouse, so session 8 has a date in the deposit for every mouse, R6 included (its training sessions are in the deposit, not the dandiset). Over all trials before session 8, 3.5% of the rare morph mice's trials are intermediate (training-intermediate-fraction above), and the rare prior holds 0.183 of its mass between 0.15 and 0.85 units, against 0.256 for the prior from the dandiset's imaged trials that the earlier run used. The frequent prior hardly changes (0.411 against 0.419). The earlier run's priors are kept as a variant labelled "earlier run", to show what the answer changed; they do not decide.

# Per-session Q estimates and Delta D_KL (M9 to M11), for the readings the claims use.
def session_q(sf, trials, anchors=M.MAP_ANCHORS_FH):
    t = M.transform_sf(sf, trials["morph"].to_numpy(), anchors)
    return M.q_unnorm(t, trials["unit"].to_numpy())


def can_sf(s):
    return (s["trials"].morph == 0).sum() >= 2 and (s["trials"].morph == 1).sum() >= 2


for s in pop + [x for x in sfs if can_sf(x)]:
    s["qu"] = session_q(s["sf"], s["trials"])
    s["q"] = M.normalise_rows(s["qu"])
    s["dkl"] = {lik: M.delta_dkl(s["q"], POST[(lik, "rare")], POST[(lik, "frequent")]) for lik in M.LIKELIHOODS}
    s["dkl_last"] = M.delta_dkl(s["q"], POST_LAST["rare"], POST_LAST["frequent"])
    s["dkl_img"] = M.delta_dkl(s["q"], POST_IMG["rare"], POST_IMG["frequent"])
    if "sf_norm" in s:
        s["q_norm"] = M.normalise_rows(session_q(s["sf_norm"], s["trials"]))
        s["dkl_norm"] = M.delta_dkl(s["q_norm"], POST[("methods var 8.23", "rare")], POST[("methods var 8.23", "frequent")])
bad = sum(M.dkl_rows(POST[("methods var 8.23", g)][M.ROWS], s["q"][M.ROWS])[1] for s in pop for g in ("rare", "frequent"))
print("grid points left out for Q = 0 where P > 0:", bad)

grid points left out for Q = 0 where P > 0: 0

Result: not reproduced. The step share (the largest fall between neighbouring S-tilde values over the whole fall, mean of the S-tilde = 0 and = 1 rows of each mouse's binned matrix) is 0.605 for rare morph mice (0.485 to 0.792) and 0.563 for frequent morph mice (0.434 to 0.749); the difference, 0.042, lies inside the 2.5 to 97.5 percentiles of the mouse permutations (-0.116 to 0.116). No mouse row has a share above 1, so clipping the share changes nothing. The rare morph rows fall mostly between S-tilde 0.25 and 0.5 (0.439 to 0.339) and the frequent morph rows fall more evenly, but the measure the criterion names does not separate the groups.

Result: not reproduced. In five of the six named sessions the S-tilde = 0.25 trials include SF values on both sides of 0.5 (R1 session 8: 5 above and 15 below; R2 session 13: 3 and 17; R3 session 9: 1 and 19; R4 session 11: 1 and 15; R6 session 10: 4 and 5). In R5 session 8 all 16 lie below 0.5 (0.424 to 0.465). The criterion asks all six and names no partial outcome, so it is not met. The session numbers are the file days. R5's file of day 8 is also the 8th task-track date of R5 in the deposit, so it is R5's session 8 under either numbering (vr-deposit-link); for the other five mice the date ordinal is one or two higher than the file day. Most other rare sessions (18 of 20) also have S-tilde = 0.25 trials on both sides.

fig3f-zscored-difference-at-025¶

After z-scoring within session, trial-by-trial population similarity differs significantly between rare and frequent morph mice for S-tilde = 0.25 trials.

In [10]:
def zdiff(key, mouse_z=False, rare=RARE, freq=FREQ):
    if mouse_z:
        per = {m: M.zscore_matrix(np.nanmean([s[key] for s in pop if s["mouse"] == m], axis=0)) for m in rare + freq}
    else:
        per = {m: np.nanmean([M.zscore_matrix(s[key]) for s in pop if s["mouse"] == m], axis=0) for m in rare + freq}
    return M.mouse_permutation(per, rare, freq)

fig4-sf-stable-along-track¶

Position-wise SF shows stable clustered representations along the whole track in rare morph mice and a spectrum in frequent morph mice; remapping happens soon after the trial starts and stays as the mouse runs.

fig6a-dkl-sign¶

Delta D_KL of each session's Q estimate took the expected sign (negative for rare, positive for frequent) in 41 of 45 sessions and in every session of 9 of 12 mice; across mice, rare -0.88 +- 0.23 and frequent 0.50 +- 0.11 (mean +- s.e.m.), a significant difference.

In [12]:
def fig6a_summary(values, label):
    d = pd.DataFrame([{"mouse": s["mouse"], "group": s["group"], "day": s["day"], "dkl": v} for s, v in zip(pop, values)])
    d["expected"] = np.where(d.group == "rare", d.dkl < 0, d.dkl > 0)
    per = d.groupby("mouse").dkl.mean()
    every = d.groupby("mouse").expected.all()
    obs, perms = M.mouse_permutation(per.to_dict(), RARE, FREQ)
    r, f = per[RARE], per[FREQ]
    out = {"reading": label, "sessions expected sign": f"{int(d.expected.sum())} of {len(d)}",
           "mice every session": int(every.sum()), "rare mean": round(r.mean(), 3), "rare sem": round(r.sem(), 3),
           "frequent mean": round(f.mean(), 3), "frequent sem": round(f.sem(), 3), "difference": round(obs, 3),
           "perm range": (round(perms.min(), 3), round(perms.max(), 3)), "outside range": bool(M.outside_range(obs, perms))}
    return out, d

fig6bc-pooled-dkl¶

Q estimates pooled over all sessions and mice approximate the posterior of the matching condition (Delta D_KL rare -0.44, frequent 0.42).

In [13]:
def group_q(mice, reading, sess=pop):
    qs = []
    for m in mice:
        ss = [s for s in sess if s["mouse"] == m and "q" in s]
        if not ss:
            continue
        if reading == "a":
            qm = M.normalise_rows(np.mean([s["q"] for s in ss], axis=0))
        else:
            qm = M.normalise_rows(np.sum([s["qu"] for s in ss], axis=0))
        qs.append(qm)
    return M.normalise_rows(np.sum(qs, axis=0)), len(qs)


for reading in "ab":
    out = {}
    for g, mice in (("rare", RARE), ("frequent", FREQ)):
        q, n = group_q(mice, reading)
        out[g] = {lik: round(M.delta_dkl(q, POST[(lik, "rare")], POST[(lik, "frequent")]), 3) for lik in M.LIKELIHOODS}
    print(f"reading {reading} ({'mean of session Q' if reading == 'a' else 'one Q from all trials of a mouse'}):", out)
out = {g: round(M.delta_dkl(group_q(mice, "a")[0], POST_IMG["rare"], POST_IMG["frequent"]), 3)
       for g, mice in (("rare", RARE), ("frequent", FREQ))}
print("earlier run, priors from dandiset trials, reading a:", out)

fig6d-prior-reconstruction¶

Priors reconstructed from each mouse's neural data alone are closer to the ideal prior of the mouse's own condition (Delta D_KL rare -0.46 +- 0.12, frequent 0.46 +- 0.07, mean +- s.e.m. across mice), a significant group difference.

In [14]:
def prior_dkl(qu, lik="methods var 8.23", priors=prior, code=False):
    R = M.reconstruct_prior(qu, lik, code=code)
    return M.dkl(priors["rare"], R) - M.dkl(priors["frequent"], R), R

Result: not reproduced. The reconstructed priors still separate the groups: the difference of across-mouse means, -0.902, lies outside the range of all permutations, and all six frequent morph mice are positive (1.125 +- 0.076, expected 0.46 +- 0.07). But with the deposit's priors the rare morph mean is positive, 0.223 +- 0.122 (expected -0.46 +- 0.12), with only R3 (-0.033) and R6 (-0.166) negative, so the sign of the rare mean fails and the criterion's partial outcome (the test and the signs) is not met either. The earlier run's priors from the dandiset's imaged trials gave rare -0.020 and frequent 0.633; the code's likelihood widths, variants, give rare 0.480 and 0.517, frequent 1.285 and 1.379.

The ideal-observer check (the verifier's request) shows that the criterion's formula cannot give the rare sign on this design: an observer whose estimates are drawn from the rare posterior, on each mouse's own trials, gives a reconstructed-prior Delta D_KL of +0.547 on average (0.380 to 0.741), while its Q estimate gives -0.303 as expected. The paper's code computes R differently, taking Z at the grid point f and not inside the sum over fhat (SFReg at dca5a57, which printed -0.476 +- 0.132 and 0.453 +- 0.074, and the 2026 code). With that computation, a variant, the rare ideal observer gives +0.047 (-0.141 to 0.268) and the frequent one +0.502, and the data give rare -0.288 +- 0.127 (4 of 6 mice negative) and frequent 0.638 +- 0.078, the difference outside every permutation. With the 2020 code's other settings as well (likelihood width 0.3 units and the last mouse's prior), rare -0.421 +- 0.123 and frequent 0.500 +- 0.077, both within tolerance, with every mouse of the expected sign. The criterion fixes the formula of the Methods, so the outcome stays not reproduced; a question asks a reader whether the claim should follow the code (questions/plitt-2021.yaml).

map-estimate-values¶

The average MAP estimate of f_h for S-tilde = 0 trials is 11.08 under the rare and 10.64 under the frequent posterior, and for S-tilde = 1 trials 38.13 and 37.30.

edf9k-null-models-rare and edf9l-null-models-frequent¶

For rare (frequent) morph sessions, Q estimates are fit worse by the other condition's, uniform, Gaussian and multimodal prior posteriors and by a uniform posterior than by the matching posterior.

In [18]:
unif = np.ones_like(M.GRID) / len(M.GRID)
gauss = np.exp(-((M.GRID - 0.5) / 0.2) ** 2); gauss /= gauss.sum()
multi = sum(w * np.exp(-((M.GRID - M.wallmorphx(sv)) / 0.08) ** 2) for w, sv in zip((1, 1, 10, 1, 1), M.MORPHS)); multi /= multi.sum()
for lik in M.LIKELIHOODS:
  nulls = {"uniform prior": M.posterior(unif, lik), "Gaussian prior": M.posterior(gauss, lik), "multimodal prior": M.posterior(multi, lik),
           "uniform posterior": np.full((len(M.GRID), len(M.GRID)), 1 / len(M.GRID))}
  print(f"##### likelihood {lik}" + (" (main)" if lik == "methods var 8.23" else " (variant)"))
  for g, other in (("rare", "frequent"), ("frequent", "rare")):
    ss = [s for s in pop if s["group"] == g]
    own = np.array([M.mean_dkl(s["q"], POST[(lik, g)]) for s in ss])
    print(f"=== {g} sessions ({len(ss)}); mean D_KL to own posterior {own.mean():.3f}")
    allok = True
    for name, P in {f"{other} posterior": POST[(lik, other)], **nulls}.items():
        d = np.array([M.mean_dkl(s["q"], P) for s in ss])
        w = stats.wilcoxon(d - own)
        ok = w.pvalue < 0.05 and np.median(d - own) > 0
        allok &= ok
        print(f"  {name:20s}: mean D_KL {d.mean():.3f}, median null minus own {np.median(d - own):.3f}, "
              f"sessions with own closer {int((d > own).sum())} of {len(ss)}, Wilcoxon p = {w.pvalue:.2g}, holds {ok}")
    print(f"  all five hold: {allok}")

Result: edf9k reproduced; edf9l not reproduced. With the deposit's priors and the Methods likelihood, for the 26 rare morph sessions every null (frequent posterior, uniform, Gaussian and multimodal priors, uniform posterior) fits worse than the rare posterior in all 26 sessions (Wilcoxon p = 3e-08 for each). For the 21 frequent morph sessions four nulls fit worse than the frequent posterior: the rare posterior (17 of 21 sessions, p = 0.00051), the Gaussian prior (p = 9.5e-07), the multimodal prior (p = 1.3e-05) and the uniform posterior (p = 1.9e-06). The uniform prior does not (the frequent posterior is closer in 5 of 21 sessions, p = 0.12), and the criterion asks all five and names no partial outcome. The code's likelihood widths, variants, give the same outcomes: every rare test holds (p at most 0.00022), and for the frequent sessions the uniform prior again fails (p = 0.18 and 0.29; frequent posterior closer in 6 and 7 of 21) while the other four hold.

(a) The Q estimate pooled over the decision mice has Delta D_KL 0.042 over every imaged session and 0.125 over sessions 8 to N, so it is closer to the frequent posterior (with the earlier run's priors these were -0.042 and -0.006); the code's likelihood widths, variants, give 0.569 to 0.820. Reading (b) carries little evidence with the criterion's formula, which is positive even for an ideal rare observer (fig6d-prior-reconstruction); with the code's computation, under which the ideal rare observer gives +0.047 and the frequent one +0.502, the decision mice give 0.433 to 0.578 over every imaged session and 0.460 to 0.627 over sessions 8 to N, near the frequent observer. The 2020 code's sessions (5 and later), a variant, give a pooled value of 0.005 and reconstructions of 0.727 to 1.082. The per-session values are positive in 25 of 35 sessions. FD1's sessions 1 and 3 have no S-tilde = 0 or 1 trials and give no SF, and FD3 has no session after 7.

fig7-model-reproduces-remapping and fig7g-model-prior-reconstruction¶

A Hebbian network with radial basis inputs and k-winners-take-all competition, trained on stimuli drawn from the rare or frequent morph prior, gives Q estimates that match the matching posterior.

Priors reconstructed from the model's Q estimates are closer to the prior of the matching condition, though less closely matched than for the neural data.

Answer of 2026-10-22: the model runs in the code's unit (1 unit = 27.42 f_h), with input width sigma = 0.15 units (4.11 f_h, so a denominator of 0.0225 units^2), input centres from -0.1 to 1.1 units, stimulus, output and weight noise as in the code, in training and testing alike, and testing on the f_h of 1,000 evenly spaced S from -0.3 to 1.3. The earlier run's readings (no weight noise, no test noise, centres over the whole grid, the width read in f_h) are dropped. The priors are those of M7 from the deposit. fig7-model-reproduces-remapping is data: elsewhere, as it needs only the priors; fig7g-model-prior-reconstruction is data: with_inputs.

In [20]:
THETA_IN = np.linspace(-0.1, 1.1, 100)          # input centres, units (code THETA)
S_TEST = np.linspace(-0.3, 1.3, 1000)            # test morph values (code)
U_TEST = M.wallmorphx(S_TEST)                     # their stimulus values, units
KW = dict(N=100, K=20, c_y=0.01, eta=0.1, tau=0.001, w_max=5.0, sigma=0.15, stim_noise=0.1, act_noise=0.01, dw_noise=0.05)


def kwta_respond(u, W, rng, p=KW):
    """Inputs and outputs for stimuli u (units): Gaussian tuning exp(-(mu - x)^2 / sigma^2) of the
    stimulus plus noise; z = W x plus 0.01 N(0,1); the K largest z give c_y z; every other output
    0.01 times the (K+1)-th largest z times N(0,1); all rectified at 0."""
    u = np.atleast_1d(u)
    s = u + p["stim_noise"] * rng.standard_normal(u.shape)
    x = np.exp(-((THETA_IN[None, :] - s[:, None]) ** 2) / p["sigma"] ** 2)
    z = x @ W.T + p["act_noise"] * rng.standard_normal((len(u), p["N"]))
    order = np.argsort(-z, axis=1)
    zk1 = np.take_along_axis(z, order[:, p["K"]:p["K"] + 1], axis=1)
    y = p["act_noise"] * zk1 * rng.standard_normal(z.shape)
    win = np.zeros_like(z, dtype=bool)
    np.put_along_axis(win, order[:, :p["K"]], True, axis=1)
    y[win] = p["c_y"] * z[win]
    return x, np.maximum(y, 0)


def hebbian_model(prior_g, rng, p=KW):
    """Methods, Hebbian learning model, with the code's scale and noise (criterion of
    fig7-model-reproduces-remapping). Returns the unnormalised Q of the test stimuli, the number of
    test stimuli without an SF, and the mean and largest weight after training."""
    W = rng.uniform(0, 0.1, (p["N"], len(THETA_IN)))       # outputs x inputs
    for u in rng.choice(M.GRID, size=1000, p=prior_g):
        x, y = kwta_respond(u, W, rng, p)
        dW = p["eta"] * y.T @ x + p["dw_noise"] * rng.standard_normal(W.shape) - p["tau"]
        W = np.clip(W + dW, 0, p["w_max"])
    _, Y = kwta_respond(U_TEST, W, rng, p)
    c0, c1 = Y[U_TEST < 0.05].mean(0), Y[U_TEST > 0.9].mean(0)
    n = np.linalg.norm(Y, axis=1)
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        g0 = Y @ c0 / (n * np.linalg.norm(c0)); g1 = Y @ c1 / (n * np.linalg.norm(c1))
        sf = g1 / (g0 + g1)
    m0 = np.nanmedian(sf[(S_TEST >= -0.1) & (S_TEST <= 0.1)]); m1 = np.nanmedian(sf[(S_TEST >= 0.9) & (S_TEST <= 1.1)])
    t = np.clip((sf - m0) / (m1 - m0) * (1.073 - 0.094) + 0.094, M.GRID[0], M.GRID[-1])
    return M.q_unnorm(t, U_TEST.copy()), int(np.isnan(sf).sum()), float(W.mean()), float(W.max())


print("test stimuli span", round(float(U_TEST.min()), 3), "to", round(float(U_TEST.max()), 3), "units (",
      round(float(M.unit_to_fh(U_TEST.min())), 2), "to", round(float(M.unit_to_fh(U_TEST.max())), 2), "f_h ); input centres",
      round(float(M.unit_to_fh(THETA_IN[0])), 2), "to", round(float(M.unit_to_fh(THETA_IN[-1])), 2), "f_h; width",
      round(KW["sigma"] * M.UNIT_FH, 2), "f_h")

Result: fig7 reproduced; fig7g reproduced. With the code's scale and noise that the answer fixed, the network learns: the weights end with a mean of 2.25 (rare-trained) and 2.77 (frequent-trained) and reach the cap of 5. The median Delta D_KL of the 50 rare-trained models is -0.564 (interquartile range -0.614 to -0.529; all 50 below 0) and that of the 50 frequent-trained models 0.093 (0.031 to 0.200; 40 of 50 above 0), so the criterion holds; the code's likelihood widths, variants, give the same signs (rare -0.697 and -0.792, frequent 0.774 and 1.003), and so do the earlier run's priors from the dandiset's trials (-0.529 and 0.101). The test stimuli, the f_h of S from -0.3 to 1.3 as the code computes it, span 0.04 to 38.45 f_h, not 5.5 to 38.5 as the criterion says, since f_h falls again for S below -0.1 (a question asks a reader about it).

For fig7g, the averaged reconstructed prior has Delta D_KL -0.098 bits for the rare-trained and 0.626 bits for the frequent-trained models (-0.068 and 0.434 nats), both of the expected sign, and both smaller in magnitude than the neural across-mouse means of fig6d-prior-reconstruction (0.223 and 1.125), so the criterion's test passes as written. But the rare neural mean has the wrong sign: the neural reconstructions of the rare morph mice do not match the rare prior at all, so "less closely matched than for the neural data" is not shown for the rare condition. With the code's computation of R, a variant, the rare-trained models give -0.349 against a neural rare mean of -0.288, a larger magnitude, and the frequent-trained models 0.378 against 0.638. The signs hold under both computations and the comparison with the neural data holds only for the frequent condition, so the outcome was given as partially reproduced after the first verification round.

The second verification round found that label inconsistent: the criterion names no partial outcome, and the attempt applies that rule to four other claims (session-and-trial-counts, fig2eh, edf7 and edf9l). Its test as written passes on the values above: both signs as expected, and 0.098 below 0.223 and 0.626 below 1.125. Reproduced was proposed for a third round, and the third round agreed, so the outcome is reproduced. The rare half of the comparison carries little evidence: the rare neural yardstick has the wrong sign, and the Methods formula gives an ideal rare observer +0.547 on this design (ideal-observer check above).

edf3-simulated-posterior-population¶

A simulated population that stochastically encodes samples from the rare or frequent morph posterior reproduces the recorded remapping patterns.

Answer of 2026-10-22: the neurons' centres are evenly spaced over the M6 grid (0.06 to 43.9 f_h), as the earlier run already had them, and the simulated difference is that of the mean over the 1,000 simulations, with each simulation's trial-by-trial matrix z-scored over its off-diagonal entries before averaging; the mean z-scored matrices are then averaged within the S-tilde blocks. The earlier run z-scored each session's 5 x 5 block matrix instead; that is kept as a variant. The posteriors are those of the deposit's priors.

for s_ in pop:
    rows_ = np.abs(M.GRID[None, :] - s_["trials"].unit.to_numpy()[:, None]).argmin(1)
    cdf_ = np.cumsum(SIM_POST[s_["group"]][rows_], axis=1)
    cdf_ /= cdf_[:, -1:]
    flat_ = (cdf_ + np.arange(len(rows_))[:, None]).ravel()        # rows stacked into one increasing array
    SIM_SESSIONS.append((s_["mouse"], s_["n_cells"], flat_, s_["trials"].morph.to_numpy()))


def _one_thread():
    from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits
    threadpool_limits(1)


def simulate(args):
    """Sum over simulations of the binned similarity per mouse, for one reading: of the trial
    matrix z-scored over its off-diagonal entries (main), and the earlier run's z-scored 5 x 5
    block matrix (variant).

    Reading a: one sample per trial and the session's cell count; b: 45 samples (one per position
    bin) and 100 neurons. Each trial's samples come from the group posterior at the trial's f_h by
    inverse transform sampling on the grid; neuron activity is gamma(kappa, 1)."""
    reading, n_sims, seed = args
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    acc, acc_v, cnt = {}, {}, {}
    for _ in range(n_sims):
        per_mouse = {}
        for mouse, ncells, flat, morph in SIM_SESSIONS:
            T = len(morph)
            n_samp, n_neur = (1, ncells) if reading == "a" else (45, 100)
            mu = np.linspace(FH_GRID[0], FH_GRID[-1], n_neur)
            u = rng.random((T, n_samp)) + np.arange(T)[:, None]
            k = np.searchsorted(flat, u) - np.arange(T)[:, None] * len(M.GRID)
            s_fh = FH_GRID[np.clip(k, 0, len(M.GRID) - 1)]
            kappa = 2 * np.exp(-((s_fh[:, :, None] - mu[None, None, :]) ** 2) / 4.11 ** 2)
            y = rng.gamma(np.maximum(kappa, 1e-300), 1.0).reshape(T, -1)
            yn = M.unit_rows(y)
            S = yn @ yn.T
            off = ~np.eye(T, dtype=bool)
            Z = (S - S[off].mean()) / S[off].std()           # trial matrix z-scored over its off-diagonal entries
            per_mouse.setdefault(mouse, []).append((M.binned_similarity(Z, morph),
                                                    M.zscore_matrix(M.binned_similarity(S, morph))))
        for mouse, Bs in per_mouse.items():
            acc[mouse] = acc.get(mouse, 0) + np.mean([b[0] for b in Bs], axis=0)
            acc_v[mouse] = acc_v.get(mouse, 0) + np.mean([b[1] for b in Bs], axis=0)
            cnt[mouse] = cnt.get(mouse, 0) + 1
    return acc, acc_v, cnt


t0 = time.time()
sim = {}
for reading in "ab":
    jobs = [(reading, 250, 9000 + 10 * (reading == "b") + k) for k in range(4)]
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(4, initializer=_one_thread) as ex:
        parts = list(ex.map(simulate, jobs))
    n_done = sum(p[2]["R1"] for p in parts)
    for k, name in ((0, ""), (1, " variant")):
        per = {m: sum(p[k][m] for p in parts) / sum(p[2][m] for p in parts) for m in RARE + FREQ}
        diff = np.mean([per[m] for m in RARE], axis=0) - np.mean([per[m] for m in FREQ], axis=0)
        sim[reading + name] = diff
    print(f"reading {reading}: {n_done} simulations; simulated rare minus frequent, trial matrices z-scored (main):")
    print(pd.DataFrame(sim[reading], index=M.MORPHS, columns=M.MORPHS).round(3).to_string())
    print(f"  variant, block matrices z-scored (earlier run): S-tilde = 0.25 row {sim[reading + ' variant'][1].round(3)}")
obs, perms, sig = fig3f["main: smoothed deconvolved, z-scored per session"]
sig_entries = [j for j in range(5) if sig[1, j]]
print("recorded significant entries of the S-tilde = 0.25 row (fig3f):", [(M.MORPHS[j], round(obs[1, j], 3)) for j in sig_entries])
for reading in ("a", "b", "a variant", "b variant"):
    same = [bool(np.sign(sim[reading][1, j]) == np.sign(obs[1, j])) for j in sig_entries]
    print(f"reading {reading}: values {[round(float(sim[reading][1, j]), 3) for j in sig_entries]}, same sign {same}")
print(f"simulation time {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

Result: not reproduced. The recorded S-tilde = 0.25 row has two significant entries (fig3f-zscored-difference-at-025), with S-tilde 0.5 (-0.409) and 1.0 (-0.367). With the deposit's posteriors and each simulation's trial matrix z-scored before averaging, as the answer fixed, the simulated rare minus frequent difference over 1,000 simulations has the same sign at 0.5 under both readings (-0.410 with one sample per trial and the session's cell count, -0.444 with 45 samples and 100 neurons). At 1.0 it is near zero: -0.036 under reading (a), the recorded sign, and +0.030 under reading (b). The criterion asks for both readings, so it is not met. The earlier run's z-scoring of the block matrices, kept as a variant, gives -0.006 and -0.004 at 1.0 with the deposit's posteriors (the earlier run had +0.009 under both readings with the dandiset's priors).

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The priors of every posterior-based claim come from the authors' figshare deposit of all VR sessions (answer of 2026-10-22), matched to the dandiset's files through the 2026 code's mouse aliases and the trial sequences (vr-deposit-link); the fig6a, fig6bc, fig6d, map-estimate-values, edf9, edf9k, edf9l, edf10, fig7g and edf3 results are counted as with_inputs, and training-intermediate-fraction and fig7 as elsewhere. The dandiset holds 26 rare morph sessions 8 to N, two more than the paper's 24. Where the claims file leaves a reading open, every reading it names is run (speed exclusion, denominators, likelihood widths, shuffle counts, decision-mouse sessions, peak readings of edf4bc). Choices not fixed by the claims file are standard ones, named where they are made: smoothing of empty position bins by normalised convolution, the 99.9th percentile of the shuffles for the UMAP filter, an NMF iteration limit of 2,000, and the operational test of "rises" (edf1). The Hebbian model follows the parameters and noise of the paper's code, as the answer fixed; the claims file's statement that its test stimuli lie between 5.5 and 38.5 f_h does not hold for S below -0.1 (fig7 conclusion).

After the first verification round. Where a criterion names no partial outcome, a claim that holds only in part is now not reproduced (session-and-trial-counts, fig2eh, edf7, edf9l). The prior reconstruction of fig6d, edf10 and fig7g follows the Methods formula as the claims file gives it; an ideal-observer check shows that this formula gives a positive Delta D_KL even for an observer that samples the rare posterior (+0.547 on average), so it cannot show the rare sign on this design. The paper's code computes R differently (Z at the grid point f), and with the 2020 code's settings it gives values within the paper's tolerances (fig6d conclusion); this is a variant, and a question asks a reader whether the claims should follow it. Other variants added: place cells with the 2020 code's 95th-percentile signal (99.91% of decisions unchanged), a plain implementation of the shuffle (identical counts), unsmoothed place-cell similarity matrices (fig2eh passes under them), the step share clipped at 1 and per-mouse medians (edf6, fig3ab), leave-one-mouse-out classification for edf5, all three likelihoods for edf9k and edf9l, the 2020 code's decision-mouse sessions (2,662 trials, within tolerance), and the mapping of file days onto the deposit's dates (vr-deposit-link).

After the second verification round. No outcome changes. For fig7g the verifier found the partial outcome inconsistent with the rule above, since its criterion names no partial outcome and its test passes as written; the verified outcome stayed, and reproduced was proposed for a third round (fig7 and fig7g conclusion). The edf5 counts vary between runs, as the UMAP layout does, and both readings hold in each run seen (edf5 conclusion). Text that quoted an earlier run is corrected.

After the third verification round. The verifier agreed with the proposal, so fig7g is reproduced. Its rare half carries little evidence, since the rare neural yardstick has the wrong sign (fig7 and fig7g conclusion).

What was found about the dataset. The version pinned holds all 16 mice; the 2021 versions hold 10. Every file holds only the imaged trials; the non-imaged trials and the sessions without imaging (2, 4 and 6) are not in the dandiset, though the paper's priors and its training statistics need them. The authors' figshare deposit holds them, but neither the dandiset nor the paper names it; its sessions link to the dandiset's files exactly, through the mouse aliases of the 2026 code, which the dandiset does not record. The deposit also holds sessions with the imaging flag that have no file in the dandiset (26 for the 12 mice, 12 of them R6's). The files hold imaging sessions 5 and 7 (and R4's session 6), which the paper does not describe, and F6's session 5 has 4,103 cells, above the paper's range. FD3 has no session after 7, so the decision-mouse counts cannot match the paper's under the claims file's readings. For R1 to R4, R6 and F4 the deposit holds one more task-track date before session 8 than sessions 1 to 7 (two more for R6), so the file day is one or two lower than the ordinal of the session's date in the deposit. session_start_time is the date of conversion (2026), not of the recording. FD1's sessions 1 and 3 hold continuous morph values. The place cells stored in the JSON annotation (the authors' 2026 code) give fractions like this attempt's and far above the paper's. No recording is deposited twice, and the activity shares the clock of the position in every session.
